idle: Half the crates on these quays are Federation. Nobody asks what's in them. Nobody wants to be the one who asks.
They fenced off Pier 9 in the spring. The trucks go in full and come out hosed down. Nobody fishes near it now.
Ships from across the Empire used to tie up here. Alexandria, Carthage, Londinium. Now it's Federation freighters or nothing.
Three troopers searched my nets for an hour yesterday. They found fish. They seemed disappointed.
The Federation pays dockers in vouchers. You can't buy fish with vouchers. I've tried.
You're not a docker. Dockers watch the cargo, not the guards. Keep walking and nobody will ask.
The canals still run clean down to the sea. About the only thing in the Porto they haven't put a number on.
Curfew horn goes at nine now. The night boats used to come in by lantern. Now they come in early or not at all.
Mind the legionary by the bollards. He's had a bad week, and he's looking for someone to share it with.
Lucretia counts the trucks off the dock road. Everyone knows it. Nobody knows who she sells the count to.
We had a harbormaster who knew every boat by the sound of its bell. They resettled him. The new one reads off a screen.
The sea doesn't care who runs Napoli. Some days that's a comfort.
nervous: They've closed the quays. Every crate, every boat, every pocket. Please, go and stand somewhere else.
They're turning the warehouses inside out. Whatever they're looking for, I don't want to be standing next to it.
Sirens all along the harbor. Anyone caught talking to you goes on the next truck. Walk away.
They're pulling people off the boats and checking hands for calluses. Yours wouldn't pass. Go.
The legionaries' radios keep saying stranger. You're a stranger. Please, not near my boat.
Every uniform on the dock road is jumpy. Somebody's going to get shot on these quays.
My boat's been searched twice already. I can't afford a third, and I can't afford you.
rumors: Dockers lifted a crate off a Federation truck last month and hid it by the water near here. Nobody's dared go back for it.
My uncle hid his savings from the customs men among the cargo on this quay. He never said where. He didn't get the chance.
A fisherman kept a stash by the canal steps round here. The trucks got him first. Better you find it than them.
Smugglers still use the old hiding places in the Porto. Under a loose stone, behind a stack. Look where nobody looks.
A legionary skimmed cargo for a year and stashed it round these warehouses. They moved him to the Castel before he could sell it.
I heard there's a bag of Imperial coin tucked under one of the quays nearby. Not my business. Could be yours.

idle: They call it Spaccanapoli because it splits the city in half. Now it's split again, into checkpoints every two hundred paces.
Two thousand years without a single car on this street. Then the Federation brought its trucks, and now the marble's cracking.
The Valerii have kept a house on this street for nine hundred years. A Federation major lives in it now. They have the attic.
Federation inspectors take samples of my stock every Thursday. In eighteen months they've never once sent back a result.
Walk the upper promenade if you want to see the city. Walk the lower one if you'd rather the city didn't see you.
The roses along the Via were planted for the Emperor's visit when I was small. Someone still waters them. Not the Federation.
Every shutter on this street used to be open by eight. Now some never open at all. Taken, or hiding. You don't knock to ask.
My mother wears crimson to market, and every day a trooper asks what it means. It means she likes crimson.
The prefect used to walk the Via on festival days and shake hands. Now he rides past in a Federation car and doesn't look out.
Forty years on this street, and now I need a pass to visit my sister across the Via.
The old families still dress for dinner. Cream and black, every night, curfew or not. It's how they say no.
Commander Hale's name is on every notice on the Via. Nobody I know has ever seen his face. Nobody wants to.
nervous: They've shut both ends of the Via. Nobody in, nobody out. Don't stand next to me.
Troopers on the promenades, legionaries in the shops. They're searching everyone. I can't be seen with you.
Move along, please. They took a man off this corner an hour ago for asking the time.
The great houses on the Via have barred their doors. That means the Federation's hunting someone. Is it you? Don't tell me.
My shop's closed. I'm closed. Please go, before they look this way.
Every checkpoint on the Via is doubled, and they're pulling people out of the arcades. Go home, if you've got one.
They've checked my papers three times in an hour. They're good papers, and my hands are still shaking. Go, please.
rumors: Servants carried things out of the Valerii house the night before the Federation moved in. Some of it's in a courtyard nearby.
A jeweler on the Via bricked up his best stock rather than register it. He's gone now. The wall's still here somewhere.
Shopkeepers hide the good stock from the requisition men. Under the arcade, behind the planters. Look past the roses.
My aunt swears there's family silver hidden by a fountain along here. She swears a lot of things. This one might be true.
Someone left a bundle down a side passage off the Via and never came back for it. If it's still there, it's yours.
Every old family on this street hid a strongbox for bad times. These are bad times, and some families aren't here to open theirs.

idle: Two hundred steps from the bottom of the lane to my door, and the Federation still finds the breath to climb them.
Everyone in the Quartieri knows everyone. That used to be a comfort. Now it's a list.
The Ferraro boy was taken in the spring. His mother asks every legionary on these steps where he went. None of them know.
Lucca's the best gunsmith in Napoli, and the kindest. He fixes their pistols so they leave him be. Nobody holds it against him.
Someone's always at a window in the Quartieri. Usually it's a grandmother. Usually.
Legionaries won't come up the narrow lanes after dark. Troopers will. That's one way to tell them apart.
My neighbor and I pass bread across the lane, balcony to balcony. Last week it was her son's papers, an hour before the search.
They've painted a number on every door in the Quartieri. Mine's 4-117. Nobody's ever asked my name.
Curfew bell rings at nine, but up here we're in by eight. You can't run on these steps.
Federation engineers came to meter our courtyard fountain. We told them it was broken. It's run fine for three hundred years.
New face on the lane. Nobody's said anything yet. Nobody will, if you keep moving.
Washing tells you everything up here. Black on the line means a funeral. No washing at all means the trucks came.
nervous: They're going door to door. Every courtyard, every stair. Please, not my door.
Shutters are closing all down the lane. Everyone up here knows what that means. Get inside somewhere, or keep going.
Don't stop here. Every window on this lane is watching, and not all of them are friendly.
They're dragging people out on the lane below. I've got children upstairs. Please, just go.
There are troopers on the steps. They don't climb up here for nothing. Whatever you did, take it somewhere else.
Legionaries are asking who's new on the lane. I won't say. Someone will.
If they find you in my courtyard, it's my family on the truck. Please.
rumors: My cousin hid something in one of these courtyards before they took him. I can't go looking. Too many windows.
There's a dead drop somewhere in these lanes. Whoever used it stopped coming. Up here, that usually means a truck.
The widow Capasso kept her pension under a flagstone in a courtyard near here. She's been resettled. The flagstone hasn't.
Somebody stashed a parcel up a dead-end lane round here, behind the washing. Not mine. I'd remember.
One legionary hid his pay near the old fountain before the Federation audited his barracks. Now he's too scared to fetch it.
Families up here keep a little something hidden for when the trucks come. Not everyone got to use theirs. Try the courtyards.

idle: I clean the officers' floors. They step over me like I'm furniture. Furniture hears a lot.
I cook for the whole garrison. They hate every meal and leave nothing on the plate. Soldiers are the same on every Earth.
The commander keeps to the minute. You could set the kitchen clocks by his boots on the stairs.
Don't go near the holding block. We're not even allowed to carry water there now. The troopers do it themselves.
My grandfather brought me here when it was a museum. Same halls. Different exhibits.
I file the intake sheets. I don't read them. I decided very early on not to read them.
They pay us in vouchers and one hot meal. Some of us only stay to hear whose name comes up next.
Not on the kitchen roster, are you? Carry something and walk like you're late. Everyone in here is.
They count the cutlery every night. They've never once counted the cleaners.
Twelve hours a day polishing boots for the people who took my brother. It's work. Work keeps my family off the list.
The trucks leave before dawn. You hear the engines from the kitchens. After a month you stop hearing them.
Nobody shouts in here. The troopers write things down. That's worse.
nervous: There's an alarm on. If they see me talking to you, I'll be in the holding block by supper. Please.
They've locked the kitchens and they're checking every face against the roster. Yours isn't on it. Go.
Don't look at me. Don't talk to me. They're watching the staff.
The troopers are running. They never run. Whatever's happening, I'm not part of it.
They're taking the staff into the yard one at a time. If they ask me, I've never seen you. Please make that true.
I've got a pass, a tray and three children. I'm not losing any of them over you. Walk on.
Every door's being checked twice. Get out of my corridor, please. Now.
rumors: Troopers skim rings and watches off the intake and stash them round these courtyards. Nobody's supposed to know.
When the cohort handed the Castel over, their quartermaster hid the mess silver somewhere in the grounds. The cooks swear to it.
A clerk who was taken last month kept a stash near the barracks. We all know about it. None of us will touch it.
There's a box under the steps in one of the yards. The trooper who put it there was shipped home. Or worse.
The cleaners say there's museum gold still bricked up somewhere in these walls. Nobody's had the nerve to look.
Kitchen staff stash what they lift from the officers' mess somewhere near the parade ground. Help yourself. They'd want you to.

flee: They're shooting! Get off the street!
Leave it, leave it, just run!
They'll take us all for this! Run!
Shut the doors! Shut the doors!
cowering: Please. I didn't see anything. I didn't see your face.
Is it over? Tell me it's over.
Don't hurt me. I've got nothing worth taking.
Stay away from me. Wherever you go, the shooting follows.
Whoever started this, it's the rest of us who'll pay for it. I hope it was worth it.
I'm staying right here until the boots are gone. Leave me alone.
